newsitem.title: UK: WORLD BONDS-Europe's books improve but market wary.
newsitem.headline: WORLD BONDS-Europe's books improve but market wary.

text.p: A trend towards lower deficits in Europe has curbed debt supply in recent years but bond investors may not automatically reap the rewards, analysts said on Friday.

Determining where yields should be and where they are heading is a lifelong obsession for debt analysts, and it does not just boil down to a case of supply and demand, they said. Andrew Bevan, senior bond economist at Goldman Sachs in London, said that in his model yields in core Europe were significantly below fair value and he questioned whether the fiscal improvement witnessed justified this. "It could be that the market is pricing in a heck of a lot more (fiscal tightening) from here, but to justify bond yields trading as far below fair value as we think they are would have to imply a set of assumptions about European fiscal policy that wouldn't really be tenable," Bevan said.

A Reuters study of official European forecasts showed at least nine, and possibly more, of 13 countries examined plan lower deficits. But actual funding needs are mixed due to issues such as redemptions that need to be refunded in 1997.
Still, analysts welcomed the trend and said the current low yield environment was tied to some extent to deficit reductions.
Mark Fox, chief European strategist at Lehman Brothers in London, said the trend was a definite plus for markets.

He said Italy, where yields fell dramatically throughout 1996 and the spread against Bunds converged, was a good example because it showed that BTPs' gains were not down solely to optimism over European Economic and Monetary Union (EMU).
The 10-year BTP/Bund spread is currently 165 basis points, compared with 475 at the start of last year.
"Imagine if Italy had produced a budget deficit of eight percent of GDP last year. Would anyone have believed in narrowing spreads simply because of EMU?" Fox said.
"The expectation of fiscal policy management in the future has to be linked with current results to make a market believe in a country," Fox said.
Bevan said one reason for the market's warm reaction to sound fiscal policy stemmed from its implication on the main factor for bond markets -- inflation.
"The dominant factor is really inflation, but ultimately there's a link there," he said. "There is a linkage between fiscal and monetary policy."
High debtor countries in the past have monitised their debt, an inflationary practice which robs investors of real yield.

Bevan said Goldman's model, which includes assumptions about real and nominal short-term rates and inflationary expectations as well as fiscal progress, estimated French and German yields were too low.

In pure supply terms, the Reuters study showed several countries would have higher funding needs despite lower deficits. These included France, Finland, Italy and Spain as they grappled with the legacy of previous fiscal patterns and had to redeem old bonds maturing in 1997.
David Brickman, European economist at Yamaichi International here, said France was a particular worry in terms of supply.
"I'm very concerned about France," Brickman said.
He said that of the French franc debt auctions so far this year, there had been seven different tranches, six of which had bid to cover ratios of less than two.
French debt outperformed benchmark German debt through much of last year, helped by continued domestic demand.
But with plans to encourage more equity holdings by pensions, and worries about future supply being digested, this trend could be at risk, Brickman said.
French 10-year debt currently yields 14 basis points less than German Bunds.
